descriptors.definition: Direct product profitability measures retail profitability by deducting directly attributable product costs from gross margin to account for indirect overhead, storage, and handling expenses. It relates indirect costs to goods according to their resource usage rather than relying solely on bought-in cost versus selling price margins.
inclusion: Warehouse costs including labor, space, and insurance
Transport costs including labor, fuel, and vehicle maintenance
Store costs and inventory financing costs
exclusion: Organization-level indirect costs not linked to product activity or movement
nearby_distinctions: Traditional gross margin only deducts bought-in cost of goods, ignoring store-level and handling indirect expenses.

descriptors.definition: Customer profitability analysis utilizes activity-based costing to assign service and support costs to specific customer segments based on their unique activity profiles. It enables organizations to identify which customers erode or contribute to overall profitability by revealing the true cost to serve them.
inclusion: Cash withdrawals, statement requests, and returned checks for banks
Special transport and rush order handling costs for manufacturers
exclusion: General organizational overheads not traceable to specific customer activity profiles
nearby_distinctions: Differs from product costing by focusing on activity consumption patterns of individual buyers rather than units produced.

descriptors.definition: This analysis provides suppliers with visibility into which customer accounts contribute to or erode overall enterprise profitability. It establishes a factual basis for constructive commercial dialogues between buyers and sellers to improve operating margins.
inclusion: Evaluation of quantity discounts and delivery discounts against actual fulfillment costs
exclusion: Arbitrary allocation of selling expenses without activity tracking
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on actionable insights from customer-specific margins rather than macro revenue totals.

descriptors.definition: Activity-based costing addresses modern manufacturing environments characterized by intense global competition and heavy workplace automation. It replaces labor-centric cost allocations with accurate tracking of non-unit level overhead costs such as setups and inspections.
inclusion: Computer-aided design and manufacturing support overheads
Setup and inspection cost pools
exclusion: Traditional volume-based allocation methods relying solely on direct labor hours
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on automated support and indirect equipment usage rather than traditional labor-intensive direct costing.

descriptors.definition: Activity-based management applies cost information gathered through activity-based costing to manage operational activities efficiently and improve customer value. It adds a dynamic continuous improvement dimension to the static cost model by focusing on cost drivers and activity performance.
inclusion: Cost driver analysis
Activity analysis for value enhancement
exclusion: Static financial reporting detached from operational activity workflows
nearby_distinctions: Unlike ABC which measures activity costs, ABM utilizes that cost data to manage operational processes and drive decisions.

descriptors.definition: Designing activity-based management involves identifying cost drivers, evaluating activity value, and performing comparative performance analyses against benchmarks. It organizes processes into activity cost pools to eliminate waste and optimize resource utilization.
inclusion: Grouping activities into activity cost centres
Identifying non-value-added steps
exclusion: Unstructured overhead dumping without operational linkage
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on operational steps and workflow drivers rather than general ledger account classifications.

descriptors.definition: Non-value-added activities create waste, introduce delays, and consume resources without enhancing the functional quality of a product or service for customers. Common examples include moving materials, waiting periods, redundant inspections, and production scheduling.
inclusion: Unnecessary material handling
Excessive work-in-process waiting times
exclusion: Activities required to meet mandatory customer quality specifications, such as essential wine aging
nearby_distinctions: Value-added activities improve product function or customer value, whereas non-value-added activities add cost without utility.

descriptors.definition: Activity-based management applications span cost reduction, budgeting, business process re-engineering, benchmarking, and performance measurement. They align organizational operations with customer demands for lower costs, higher quality, faster response, and greater innovation.
inclusion: Process waste elimination
Activity-based budget formulation
exclusion: Purely historical financial accounting reviews lacking operational metrics
nearby_distinctions: Applies activity cost data directly to strategic enterprise initiatives rather than routine product valuation.

descriptors.definition: Cost reduction under activity-based management involves identifying expenses tied to specific activities to streamline processes or eliminate non-value-added tasks. It provides a structured vehicle for continuous process improvement by quantifying and targeting operational waste.
inclusion: Elimination of wasteful non-value-added activities
Quantification of process inefficiencies
exclusion: Arbitrary across-the-board budget cuts that ignore underlying activity drivers
nearby_distinctions: Targets specific operational workflows and task inefficiencies rather than arbitrary expense slashing.

descriptors.definition: Activity-based budgeting plans and controls expected organizational activities to derive a cost-effective budget matching forecast workloads and strategic goals. It analyzes resource inputs based on the type, quantity, and cost of work to be performed.
inclusion: Budgeting frameworks based on expected activity levels
Comparison of actual results against budgeted activity drivers
exclusion: Traditional incremental budgeting based solely on historical financial expenditure trends
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on operational workloads and activity resource demand rather than historical financial account balances.

descriptors.definition: Implementing activity-based management requires securing top management support, defining critical enterprise issues, and integrating ABC methods into core reporting systems. Successful rollouts engage actual information users within implementation teams to ensure high-level conceptual clarity.
inclusion: Incorporation of ABC methods into primary cost reporting structures
Engagement of system users during deployment
exclusion: Bottom-up accounting changes implemented without leadership alignment
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on the administrative rollout and structural integration steps rather than mathematical cost assignment.

descriptors.definition: Activity-based management provides a structured framework for cost reduction, process improvement, and effective managerial decision-making. It enables operational management to understand underlying cost drivers and prioritize the management of key resources.
inclusion: Identification of process waste elements
Clear guidance on implementing activity-based budgets
exclusion: General cost accounting reports that omit operational drivers
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on managerial control and operational optimization rather than financial valuation accuracy alone.
